title: Trustworthy AI Helper - Verify, De-risk & Showcase (Part 2 Lab)
summary: Students carry out their verification and risk check, refine and re-verify if a check fails, then argue with evidence that their helper can be trusted and reflect across the four skills.
objectives: Carry out the verification and risk check, refine the helper if a check fails, and confirm it can be trusted.
Present the Trustworthy AI Helper and reflect on the thinking used across all four skills.

worksheet.title: Week 6 - Lab - Worksheet | Trustworthy AI Helper - Verify, De-risk & Showcase (Part 2 Lab)

questions.prompt: Sam's helper says 'most of our class picked adventure'. He checks the class survey totals: adventure 7, science 11. His verification has failed. What should he do next?

options.text: Refine the helper so that its claim fits the data, then verify the claim again.
Keep the output as it is and add a note saying that it might be wrong.
Ask the helper the same question again and use whichever answer it gives.
Change the survey totals so that they agree with the helper's claim.

feedback.correct: Exactly - a failed check is useful information: you refine the helper and then re-verify, rather than keeping an output you know does not match the data.
feedback.incorrect: A failed check means the output is wrong, so warning labels, re-asking the tool, or editing the real totals all leave the mistake in place - refine the helper, then verify again.

questions.prompt: Sam's first verification failed. Put these five steps into the order he should follow to fix his helper and show that it can be trusted.

items.text: He checks the new claim against the survey totals again, and this time it matches.
He checks the helper's claim against the class survey totals.
He uses the passed check as evidence that his helper can be trusted.
He finds that the claim does not match the totals.
He changes the helper so that its claim follows the data.

feedback.correct: That is the verify-refine-re-verify loop: you can only argue that a helper is trustworthy after a check has actually been passed.
feedback.incorrect: Check first, and only then find the problem, change the helper, and check again - the trust argument comes last, because it rests on the check that finally passed.

questions.prompt: Which of these count as evidence that a helper can be trusted? Choose all that apply.

options.text: I checked the claim 'adventure was picked most' against the survey totals, and it matched.
I removed the duplicate reply, ran the helper again, and now no pupil is counted twice.
The helper answered very quickly and never hesitated.
I asked the helper whether it was sure, and it said yes.
I took the pupils' names out of the output and checked that none were left.

feedback.correct: Yes - evidence is a check you actually carried out and the result it gave, not how confident or fast the helper seemed.
feedback.incorrect: Speed and a confident 'yes' from the tool tell you nothing about whether the output is right; evidence is a check you carried out against something trustworthy, and a mitigation you applied and then re-checked.

questions.prompt: In your reflection you look back across the four skills you used. Match each skill to the piece of work that shows it.

right.text: I showed that the most-picked genre in the survey is what decided the suggestion.
I found two replies from the same pupil and removed one before using the data.
I checked the claim against the survey totals and took the pupils' names out of the output.
My first instruction gave a vague answer, so I rewrote it to ask for one book and a reason.

feedback.correct: Well matched - each skill leaves a different trace in your work, which is what makes a reflection specific rather than vague.
feedback.incorrect: Cleaning the data is data quality, rewriting the instruction is prompt refinement, showing which data decided the output is data influence, and checking a claim or reducing a risk is verification and risk.

questions.prompt: Leila's helper suggests one book for the whole class, and all of her checks passed. A friend now wants to use the same helper to label which pupils are 'good readers' and which are not. Which rule best fits what this lesson teaches about risk?

options.text: Use the helper to suggest a book for the class, but not to label individual pupils, because a wrong or unfair output would judge a real person.
Use it for both, as long as you tell people that an AI made the decision.
Use it for both, because the data behind the helper has already been checked once.
Stop using the helper altogether, because any output it gives could turn out to be wrong.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the same helper carries a much bigger risk when its output labels a person, so the sensible rule limits it to the use where a mistake is easy to spot and easy to undo.
feedback.incorrect: Passing checks for one job does not make a helper safe for every job - announcing that an AI decided, or checking the data once, does not undo the harm of unfairly labelling a pupil, and the book suggestion was already shown to be trustworthy.

formative.targets: Integrated mastery confirmation - GE (verification and risk) with CU, SD, CE from earlier, plus reflection
